I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields. I would not spread myself across many crops this year. In Quzhou County, wheat-maize rotation is the normal high-yield system, summer brings most of the rain, and winter wheat is the crop that needs more irrigation, so this is the safest and easiest plan for me to manage with my labor and experience. I will use better seed, not save my own seed, because I want a steadier stand and more reliable yield. I will keep fertilizer moderate, not chase extreme output, because water is always a real limit here and too much input raises cost and risk. For wheat I will irrigate a few key times and manage weeds and disease carefully; for maize I will rely mostly on summer rain, sow quickly after wheat harvest, and keep field work simple. This matches the long-running Quzhou wheat-maize system described for the county and its climate: [Nature/Scientific Reports](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep41587), [PMC version](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/), [MDPI Quzhou water-demand table](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-445X/12/2/462).

decision.reasoning_summary: I will plant winter wheat and summer maize in rotation on the same 10 mu because that is the most familiar, stable, and locally suitable system for me in Quzhou County. I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed for more even emergence and steadier yield. I will keep fertilizer at a moderate level, irrigate wheat three times at key stages, and give maize only one irrigation if rainfall is short, because summer rain usually supports maize better than wheat. I will use rotary tillage before wheat and no-tillage direct seeding for maize after wheat harvest so I can save time, keep the season tight, and manage the work with less complexity.
